@@137738613 <h> Carney says national unity council will study surge in antisemitism <p> OTTAWA -- The new national unity council will assess what is driving antisemitism in Canada and improve research and data collection on hate incidents , Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday . Speaking at a synagogue in Toronto , Carney said " antisemitism has surged to levels not previously seen in the postwar period , " noting incidents including the firebombings of synagogues and bullets fired at Jewish schools . He said more than two-thirds of all religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025 were directed at Jewish Canadians , who make up only one per cent of the population . Combatting the problem starts with an admission that currently Canada is " failing Jewish Canadians , " he said . He then listed off a number of tasks assigned to the new advisory council on rights , equality and inclusion , announced in February . That includes studying " the nature , scale and drivers of antisemitism " in Canada , and to improve research and data collection on hate incidents . Carney said the antisemitism crisis in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ response . " He said the government is fully committed to that response . Carney 's announcement comes less than a month after Toronto police responded to a call about three " visibly " Jewish community members being shot at with an imitation firearm . The spike in antisemitic incidents follows the October 2023 attack by Hamas militants on Israel , which prompted Israel to bomb the Gaza Strip . Israel has drawn widespread condemnation over its aid restrictions and destruction of infrastructure in Gaza . Speaking to reporters Monday , Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Carney should offer the Jewish community " a big apology . " " Mark Carney should lay out an apology to the Jewish community for the violence , the terror and the fear that his party and his government have allowed to happen over the last decade , " he said . Criticizing Liberal policies , Poilievre said Canada needs to secure its borders against " illegal immigration " and " deport visitors who are participating in these acts of terror and violence on our streets . " " We need the government to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said . " I would encourage Liberals to stop the divisive rhetoric and work on uniting Canadians . Miller told reporters the advisory council would recognize Islamophobia and antisemitism but focus on national unity and " trying to bring people together . " The government announced at the time it would drop its stand-alone federal envoys to combat Islamophobia and antisemitism and fold the two positions into the new advisory council , composed of prominent academics , experts and community leaders . A Senate committee studying antisemitism in April called on Carney to restore the antisemitism envoy . Currently , the Criminal Code has hate propaganda provisions on advocating genocide , public incitement and wilful promotion of hatred , and wilful promotion of antisemitism . It also recognizes as an offence mischief motivated by bias , prejudice or hate . But other hate crimes , such as those involving homicide or assault , do n't have specific offences in the Criminal Code . Instead , hate is identified as an aggravating factor at sentencing . Among other new provisions , C-9 would create a specific hate crime offence for acts motivated by hatred . Statistics Canada reported in March an increase in reported hate crimes between 2018 and 2024 of 169 per cent , from 1,817 reported incidents up to 4,882 . " Government and law enforcement must address the drivers of this crisis , including radicalization , promotion of terrorism , and terrorist entities operating here in Canada , " Shack said in a news release Sunday . " The prime minister has an opportunity to set the tone from the highest office to make clear that nothing can justify the hatred , intimidation , and violence Jewish Canadians are experiencing and that every tool at the government 's disposal will be used to confront it . @@137743115 <h> Montreal Holocaust Museum launches campaign to combat antisemitism using the voices of survivors ' children and grandchildren <p> A poster , part of a campaign by the Montreal Holocaust Museum , which reads : Marek came to Canada in 1948 after surviving the Holocaust . Today his granddaughter is facing antisemitism while managing the Holocaust Museum 's social media . Listen to her story . ( Photo supplied ) . . <p> When Sarah Fogg posts on the Montreal Holocaust Museum ( MHM ) social media accounts about her grandfather Marek , who came to Canada in 1948 , one of approximately 40,000 Holocaust survivors who rebuilt their lives in this country , she 's met with a torrent of replies that include photos of ovens . <p> " Being at the museum , I 'm exposed to probably a lot more than other people , " says Fogg , communications director for the museum . " It 's frustrating and a lot of it is hidden behind this criticism of Israel . Of course you can criticize a country , that 's not the problem . When you @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Auschwitz uniform , it 's a different story . " <p> Hers is one of several testimonials featured in a new bilingual public awareness campaign to combat antisemitism using voices of survivors ' descendants to recount their own experiences . <p> Thanks to an MHM investment and grant from Canadian Heritage , the museum rolled out its multi-faceted effort to record descendant testimonies , develop a new educational workshop for adults and professionals , and launch a major antisemitism awareness campaign . <p> The project also bolsters the MHM 's world-class oral history collection by recording descendants ' testimonies with excerpts available on the Museum 's YouTube channel , where viewers can better understand their unique perspectives on contemporary situations of hate , and the complex legacies they carry as descendants of Shoah survivors . <p> The public awareness component ran mid-April to early May with ads in multiple print and online platforms , as well as on 40 large street level posters and bus shelter displays at major transit hubs , and in targeted areas of the city , to sensitize the public to the persistence of antisemitism . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about digital ads is that we get information about clicks and engagement right away , " said Fogg , noting for example , one French news site ad garnered more than 400 clicks , and another 's ad received more than 120,000 views . While street advertising is harder to tally , website statistics show clear spikes in visits and engagement , bringing nearly 40,000 visitors to the MHM website and page dedicated to combatting antisemitism following the roll-out , along with social media posts generating over 31,500 views . <p> " The goal was to have as many eyes on it as possible , " Fogg told The CJN , " because antisemitism is n't only a Jewish problem . We did n't need to raise awareness in Jewish neighbourhoods , although it would be nice to publicize what we 're doing , of course , but we really prioritized non-Jewish areas , downtown and east Montreal , the Plateau , Mile End , areas like that . " <p> Passersby were invited to learn more via QR codes to videos about descendants ' experiences of antisemitism and living @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to date been viewed more than 4,000 times . <p> A big surprise says Fogg , was that campaign materials on the street were n't vandalized . " You expect graffiti all the time . I was expecting the ads to be defaced too . It would 've been painful seeing pictures of our grandparents treated that way , but it did n't happen . " <p> They boosted another museum ad on social media " and comments were horrific . We talked about this and for a while we hid the comments , but eventually we decided to leave them visible . If someone is going to post something hateful , we do n't need to help them hide their identity . It 's evidence of what 's happening . " <p> Meanwhile , the street and print ads invited Montrealers to take advantage of free Sunday admissions at the museum , a promotion since January and continuing until the end of June . @@137743116 <p> A canary living its best life . Photo credit : steve b , CC0 , via Wikimedia Commons <p> Having devoted much of my time in a French doctoral program at New York University to studying antisemitism , it has been a strange experience to see the Maison Fran ? aise of NYU now regularly hosting talks on what as recently as the 2010s felt like a deeply unchic subject . When I was in the program , Jewish Studies had turned away from the " lachrymose , " and the rest of academia was shall we say lukewarm where the study of anti-Jewish oppression was concerned , in keeping with progressivism generally . <p> A part of me is pleased to see that topics I knew to be important are now recognized . But there 's a broader context , one in which it is not necessarily good -- for Jews or generally -- that antisemitism is now a hot topic . I mean there 's the obvious reason it 's bad : the spiking antisemitism that has inspired the general public to take an interest in what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a thing of the past . But there 's more to it as well . <p> In The Chronicle of Higher Education , a feature by Stephanie M. Lee , " The Fight Over Antisemitism Studies , " describes tensions surrounding the emergence of centres and even degree programs aimed at researching and combatting antisemitism . At just the moment when , at Trump 's behest , American higher ed is otherwise chucking Oppression Studies programs and activist scholarship of the researching and combatting variety , there 's this one sort of woke that is for some reason permitted , and it 's the one where Jews and only Jews do count . As with Trump 's general anti-antisemitism doings , it is not always entirely clear they are beneficial to Jews . <p> There 's a lot of interest in the Chronicle article , but spot the strangeness of this passage : <p> " At some of the country 's most prestigious universities , the antisemitism-research apparatus is taking the form of new centers . In November 2023 , NYU announced that it was establishing the Center for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moment that cries out for new study , new insights , and new solutions to combatting this age-old hatred . ' The moment came less than six weeks after the Hamas attacks and a day after three students sued the university for allegedly tolerating anti-Jewish discrimination . That December , following a flurry of Gaza protests , the University of Michigan announced it would start the Wallenberg Institute , named for a Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews during the Holocaust . In January 2024 , the University of Toronto said it would build an antisemitism-studies lab . " <p> The inclusion of a university in Canada in this list of prestigious American universities would seem to be attributing to Trump a reach beyond what he has . <p> This strange digression into 51st-state-ism notwithstanding , it 's a compelling story . ' Studies ' fields have long been a source of contention . Their strength is interdisciplinarity , but they get criticized for not grounding the students in any existing discipline . I have a joint doctorate in French and French Studies and could go further into the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an issue in French Studies , but anything with " studies " in the name often stands accused of being extra-woke , as versus traditional academia , with its ( imagined ) absence of politics . <p> Much like censorship accusations get hurled , not unfairly , in all directions , so too the claim that a subfield is insufficiently rigorous . For one culture-wars team , academia as it currently exists , or did prior to Trump 's whittling away at it , is a mess of fluff , jargon , and activism . A highfalutin version of DEI at best , and at worst , an illiberal not to mention antisemitic cult . For another , there is this real if flawed entity , academia , currently being challenged by what are in effect right-wing clown colleges : the University of Austin ( aka the Bari Weiss university ) , the De Santis-revamped New College of Florida , and now , a network of " studies " departments and institutes aimed at training the next generation of anti-antisemitism consultants . <p> It can feel a bit indulgent , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ certain topics could be study areas but not disciplines . Is n't it all arbitrary how these things get classified ? Indeed , some of what 's meant , when people say that a field is n't worthy of existing , is dismissiveness . It 's a way of gently or pretentiously referring to someone else 's pursuit as trivial . Lee 's focus is a small program at little-known Gratz College in Pennsylvania , an online-only graduate program with no pretense of training future professors . Does it matter if Gratz College offers an Antisemitism Studies degree ? Let them offer Antisemitism Studies with a minor in Philosemitic Basketweaving . A part of me wants to say that the problem is Trump cracking down on other parts of academia , and that the answer is more of everything , including new fields . <p> But I -- a strong supporter of the academic study of antisemitism with the doctorate to show for it -- am not convinced that antisemitism itself should be a field in which anyone 's getting a degree . <p> As the focus of an academic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , book ) , antisemitism is valid , worthy , and necessary . Antisemitism is , to put it mildly , a thing in the world . Defining it , understanding where it comes from , this is an important part of understanding humanity generally and , yes , of Jewish Studies specifically . The remarkable persistence of antisemitic conspiracy theories , the staying power of Jew-hatred as an organizing principle , is massively important for understanding how the world works . There are very few Jews in the world , and rather a lot more with overpowering ideas about Jews . <p> On the Jewish Studies end , studying antisemitism is integral both to understanding what it 's like to be Jewish , and making sense of the boundaries of Jewishness itself . <p> There is a definition of Jewishness that is , in effect , you 're Jewish if antisemites consider you a Jew . I get the impulse to push back against that , to say , we can define ourselves , thanks , pointing to any number of ways Jews self-identify . But antisemitism also materially @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the last name Cohen . And this dynamic is important for understanding Jewish history . Sometimes , people in that sort of situation ' return ' to a Judaism that is effectively new to them , a trajectory explored in Katie Lynes 's moving essay for Judith . Paradoxically , antisemitism can serve as a force bringing some in from the Jewish fringes . Antisemitism can also , more straightforwardly , inspire some Jews to shed particularity and , in their lifetimes or over generations , check out . So yes , antisemitism-the-concept matters for anyone studying Jewish demography or identity . <p> The displacing of Jewish Studies itself is nevertheless concerning . And it is , in this strange political climate , what appears to be underway : <p> " Like Penn 's Steven Weitzman , the professors overseeing the new antisemitism initiatives at NYU , Toronto , and Michigan come from Jewish-studies centers and departments . It might seem a logical match , but Weitzman believes that ' antisemitism studies is really the study of non-Jewish culture . ' To understand why the Nazis exterminated 6 million Jews @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ German history and the psychology of the perpetrators . " <p> It 's not for nothing I was studying antisemitism from within a French department and not a Jewish Studies one . But I digress . <p> Antisemitism is a lens for understanding Jews . But how far does it get you ? I will set aside the question of Judaism itself , as in the religion , because it is self-evident that Antisemitism Studies would explicate neither Torah nor Talmud . Instead , I 'll stick with : how would Antisemitism Studies help you understand the sitcom Seinfeld ? It would get at why they could n't make George Costanza Jewish , and would shed light on a handful of plotlines ( shiksappeal , Uncle Leo 's paranoia , the limo-misunderstanding episode , possibly the " I had a pony " scene , definitely the " anti-dentite " coinage about people who hate dentists ) . But would it get at Jewish sensibilities , at parents-in-Florida , at Woody Allen and Philip Roth 's comedic legacies , at the importance of tracking down the right kind of babka , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on NYC public access television ? The forest would be missed for the trees if antisemitism was all you were looking at , or for , when understanding that show 's Jewish angles . <p> The part that concerns me is how it reifies the idea of Jews as a hated group . I feel this way even about the expression Jewish joy , which comes across , to me , as a protest-too-much reaction to the lachrymose . I 'm thinking more of just , Jewish normalcy . Like , imagine you send your child to Hebrew school and they come home knowing not the Aleph Bet nor the story of Passover nor the concept of tikkun olam but the precise number of Jews murdered in each European country during the Holocaust . Would anyone want that ? The this is who we are needs to precede the and we are hated . @@137747206 <p> Mark Carney chose Holy Blossom Temple -- one of Toronto 's great historic synagogues -- to deliver what may be the most direct and morally serious address on antisemitism ever given by a sitting Canadian prime minister . For that , he deserves genuine credit , and genuine engagement . <p> He was unequivocal . He said Canada 's civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians , who have been " particularly and brutally targeted . " He recognized that when this covenant fails one community , it fails us all . He announced a new Ministerial Advisory Council , committed to a four-pronged approach , and he called on every Canadian to stand up and speak out . He understood , and said plainly , that the hate targeting Jews is not equivalent to the hate directed at others . <p> All of this is welcome and necessary . And I believe the Prime Minister is sincere . <p> But there were two elephants in the room , almost completely unmentioned -- and they will ultimately undermine everything else he said . <p> The first : Israel . I understand the political logic . I do not accept the analytical one . <p> The second : the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance 's Working Definition of Antisemitism , which Canada adopted in 2019 , and its accompanying handbook . @@137875332 <p> Canada is going through a rough patch . Our best friend in the world is suddenly acting like an enemy . Our economic productivity and standard of living are lagging . Our famously livable cities are looking ragged around the edges . In two of our provinces , separatism is rearing its ugly head again . <p> But there is one way in which , for all our faults , we are doing exceedingly well . Over the past couple of generations , we have welcomed and absorbed millions of newcomers . It is the greatest success of our recent history , a glowing example in a world torn by renewed tribalism , prejudice and conflict . The 2026 World Cup is the perfect occasion to celebrate it . <p> The World Cup is the biggest event in the planet 's most popular sport . This year , as co-host with the United States and Mexico , Canada is putting on 13 matches : seven in Vancouver , six in Toronto . <p> The country that welcomed the world is welcoming the world 's game . It will be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this country will be part of a global extravaganza followed by billions . Watch parties , fan fests and victory celebrations will make Canadian streets teem with life . Throngs of visitors from soccer-mad nations as disparate as Germany and Senegal will flock to our shores . The first match , in Toronto on June 12 , will feature Canada 's own national team , playing in the tournament for only the third time , this one on home soil . <p> Yes , the ticket prices are obscene and , yes , the cost to taxpayers is outrageous : more than $1-billion , according the federal government 's Parliamentary Budget Officer . But we need this . The world needs this . <p> At its best , says Franklin Foer , the American author of How Soccer Explains the World : An Unlikely Theory of Globalization , the World Cup is " this incredible , beautiful , joyous festival of nationalism . Whatever rivalries and historic hatreds exist are expressed in a mostly harmless way . " <p> We will see that truth up close on the streets of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scale few nations have ever seen made sure of that . <p> You can find people from every corner of the world in Vancouver and Toronto -- or Calgary , Halifax and Kitchener , for that matter . The captain of Canada 's team himself , Alphonso Davies , was born in a refugee camp in Ghana after his parents escaped a civil war in Liberia . <p> The result will be a multinational celebration of the world 's most multinational sport . In France , they will be flying the French flag to support their national team ; in Algeria , the Algerian . Canadians will be waving 48 flags this World Cup : one for each contender -- Canada included . <p> When asked to make their own ' identity shields , ' Grade 4 and 5 pupils added symbols of their heritage to the mix at Toronto 's Market Lane Junior and Senior Public School . There are flags from Yemen , Antigua and Barbuda , Finland and , of course , Canada . <p> Explore the school 's environs and you 'll find tributes to many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first World Cup in 1930 . There are abut 7,600 people of Uruguayan origin in Canada . Walk further and you 'll find 51 patriotic beavers at various Old Town Toronto businesses . This one was painted by Ghanaian artists Cassandra Quaye , Emmanuel Glover and Alicom Ochere . <p> Twenty-first century Canada is a different kind of homeland . Not a " post-national state , " in Justin Trudeau 's mushy formulation -- our sense of nationhood is strong -- but a place where people can celebrate both their ancestry and their country without fear . <p> You do n't have to look hard to find the proof . I found it in a remarkable Toronto neighbourhood called the Esplanade , just around the corner from the headquarters of The Globe and Mail . <p> Tucked into a historic nook of downtown , steps from where the city was first established two centuries ago , it is a pleasant mix of townhouses , condos , apartments and co-ops holding people from all manner of incomes and backgrounds . <p> Its variety is astounding . The sandwich board for a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ garlic bread and biryani , according to your taste . <p> New arrivals from places like the Philippines or the Punjab mix with older residents from Russia , Italy , Poland and Scotland . <p> Toronto has a Little Italy , a Little Portugal and a Little India , not to mention at least two Chinatowns . The Esplanade is more like Little Everywhere . <p> To mark the World Cup , a local arts group called Jamii ( Swahili for " community " ) had an ambitious idea : take photos of people representing each of the four dozen countries playing in the tournament and put them up in the neighbourhood -- something that would be impossible in most places . The photos are now arrayed along the edge of a park named after a popular Toronto mayor , David Crombie . <p> One of them shows Jae Yang , 44 , a photographer who took some of the shots in the series himself . His parents are Korean by origin . They moved to Argentina and he grew up there , living and breathing soccer the way people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canada , where he moved two decades ago , he met a woman of Chinese ancestry who grew up in Peru . When this Asian-looking pair go up to Hispanic people and start speaking Spanish , says Mr. Yang , " they look at us like we have three heads . " <p> He will cheer for all of his " home " teams this month : South Korea 's , Argentina 's and Canada 's . He has a jersey for each . He just hopes South Korea and Argentina do n't end up playing against each other : " That would be bad . " <p> Jae Yang , featured in one of the photos around the Esplanade , took some of the other photos with people from the community . <p> Another picture in the series shows Iris Unlu , 35 . She came to Canada from Turkey in 2015 , intending to stay a few months and improve her English . She is still here , living happily with her Toronto-born partner and her big fluffy white dog . She relishes the freedom she has here @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ something she says she could not have done in Turkey . <p> Countries from every populated continent are represented in the photo project , from Austria to Australia , Sweden to Ecuador . The organizers even found a couple to represent Cura ? ao , an island in the Dutch Caribbean with a population of just 158,000 -- the smallest country ever to compete in the World Cup . <p> To Ms. Unlu , " it 's kind of crazy mind-blowing " that they could track down people from so many places . But that is Toronto ; that , increasingly , is Canada . <p> ' If Canada is a little bit smug , I think it deserves it , ' says Iris Unlu , with Jae Yang at one of the installations . Ms. Unlu moved here from Turkey more than a decade ago and says she enjoys the greater freedom . <p> Mr. Yang grew up in Argentina , which won the last World Cup in Qatar four years ago . That was the first tournament in more than three decades where Canada qualified to compete . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ return the hospitality . <p> The scale of this change is monumental . The Toronto that I grew up in in the 1950s and 1960s was a hidebound , provincial city where a dinner out meant spaghetti , checked tablecloths and wine bottles wrapped in straw . My North Toronto high school class had precisely one Chinese guy , who stuck out like a sore thumb in the sea of kids with names such as Rogers or Roberts . <p> By the time I was starting to raise a family of my own , the city , and the country , had changed beyond recognition . The waves of migrants from Southern Europe who settled in Canada after the Second World War were followed by new waves from Asia : India , Pakistan , China , the Philippines , Vietnam . <p> The downtown school my own children attended had kids from 32 countries . In today 's Toronto , seven out of 10 students in the public-school system list their race as something other than white . They and their families speak more than 100 languages . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , has kids from every background under the sun . When one teacher asked his pupils to show on a world map where their families came from , they placed stickers from Myanmar to Ukraine , Tanzania to Chile . In the school 's senior grades , 24 per cent identify as white , 19 per cent South Asian , 16 per cent East Asian , 12 per cent Black , 7 per cent Middle Eastern , 5 per cent Southeast Asian and 3 per cent Latino . Fourteen per cent list their background as " more than one . " <p> Two kids whose families fled the conflict in Sudan as refugees just enrolled . The school paired them with other Arabic-speaking students , but they are already picking up English . " Good morning , " one of them , a boy , sang out to Principal Laurie Jantzi in the stairwell this week . <p> Many of the kids are soccer fanatics , constantly kicking a ball back and forth at recess . One teacher wants to use the school foosball table to stage a kind of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the principal at Market Lane , where soccer is a passion and a pastime for many pupils . <p> Food writer Suresh Doss never stops being dazzled by this country 's diversity . For 25 years , he has been exploring it with his taste buds . <p> He came to Canada when his Sri Lankan family settled in the Toronto suburb of Scarborough . His mother and grandmother were great cooks , so he learned to love food . He made his name talking about the great restaurants you can find in strip malls on the edges of town . <p> Today , Mr. Doss says , diners can sample fantastic dishes from all over the world in every corner of Toronto . @@138080190 <p> When Bill Clinton sat down with recently elected Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in June , 1996 , the U.S. president was eager to push forward the Oslo process for peace with the Palestinians he had started three years earlier . <p> Instead , Mr. Netanyahu lectured him on the history of Israeli-Arab relations . " Who 's the fucking superpower here ? " Mr. Clinton fumed to his aides afterwards , in an unusually profane reaction to the leader of a close ally . <p> This moment , recounted by Aaron David Miller , then a U.S. State Department official working on the peace process , would prove to be a preview of Mr. Netanyahu 's relationship with four American presidents across his 18 years of intermittent rule . <p> White House frustration with such perceived intransigence led to a similar executive expletive this month when President Donald Trump , angry that Mr. Netanyahu was jeopardizing negotiations to end the war with Iran by bombing Lebanon , reamed him out over the phone . <p> " Everybody hates Israel because of this , " Mr. Trump said , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ called Mr. Netanyahu " crazy " and swore in the conversation . <p> But if the dynamic Mr. Trump is colliding with is familiar , his relationship with Mr. Netanyahu is unique in two ways : No previous U.S. president has done so much of what the Israeli leader has demanded , nor so openly given him orders and been so publicly exasperated about the difficulty of doing so . <p> Mitchell Barak , an Israeli pollster who worked for Mr. Netanyahu in the 1990s , said Mr. Trump 's frustration is " par for the course " among world leaders who have dealt with the Israeli Prime Minister . <p> " He does what he thinks is in the best interest of Israel . He does n't see anything other than the thing he thinks needs to be done right away , " Mr. Barak said of Mr. Netanyahu 's decision-making . <p> While Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu worked together to attack Iran this past February , their war aims have since diverged : Mr. Trump is trying to get out of the conflict because Iran 's shutdown @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of oil , fertilizer and other goods that must transit the waterway , while Mr. Netanyahu wants a decisive victory over the Islamic Republic and its regional proxies . <p> " The U.S. does n't want to get involved in Lebanon , Syria or Iran long term , while Netanyahu sees a real threat , " Mr. Barak said . <p> Mr. Trump has long presented himself as the most pro-Israel U.S. president ever . " <p> Also working against Mr. Netanyahu is Mr. Trump 's tight control of the Republican Party . I 'm of Montreal-Jewish heritage and have a doctorate in French so I 'd guessed what was up prior to reading , but I read it all the same . In their quest to protect Quebec from Anglophone hegemony , Jews -- Anglo-coded , if not always Anglophone ( see : Moroccans , etc. @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canadian and maybe the only North American city to rival New York in old-timey Jewish nostalgia cred , lost much of its Jewish population in the postwar years due to instability stemming from Quebec separatism . None of this ! " If the titular Arthur instead had a collation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the clear . A deeply French-Canadian-specific aspect to this story that I have not seen mentioned is that in French from France , the comment dit-on of snack bar is " snack-bar , " whereas in Quebec it 's casse-cro ? te . So if it were Arthurs Snack-Bar , sans Nosh , the owners could claim French-from-France , possibly . <p> Whether anyone other than whoever filed the original complaint is bothered about this is hard to say , though the Gazette piece mentions a smattering of online detractors . That section was amended to ensure it covers " nearly nude " images , after experts warned the original version of the bill likely would not incorporate many of the images created by Elon Musk 's Grok chatbot that proliferated on his X platform at the beginning of this year . <p> The bail bill <p> Bill C-14 , which makes it more difficult to get bail for a variety of crimes , received royal assent Monday . <p> The bill makes dozens of changes to the Criminal Code , including the introduction of a new reverse onus provision for certain offences -- meaning the accused must prove they should receive bail , rather than a prosecutor convincing a judge that bail should be denied . <p> People charged with a third violent crime , or who were convicted in the last decade of a similar violent offence involving a weapon , would also be affected by the change . <p> The law came after pressure from opposition Conservatives and most provinces following high-profile cases of violent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Lawful access <p> The government says its " lawful access " bill , C-22 , will ensure law enforcement agencies have the legal tools to prevent , investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms . <p> The Bill passed the House Thursday but it has not yet been dealt with in the Senate . <p> Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies , endangering privacy , flouting the Charter and making Canada less attractive to business . <p> The Liberals agreed to several amendments to try to allay concerns , including shortening the time electronic service providers would be required to keep digital metadata . The bill initially could have required providers to retain metadata , which can reveal a person 's location and movements , for up to one year . That has now been limited to up to six months . <p> Implementing the Liberals ' spring mini-budget <p> Bill C-30 , which passed third reading in the House of Commons on Thursday , enacts certain measures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> They include codifying the temporary break on the federal fuel excise tax into law . <p> The bill also reduces Canada Pension Plan contributions for employees and employers starting in 2027 , extends the repayment grace period for withdrawals made under the Home Buyers ' Plan and makes permanent a capital-gains tax exemption for businesses sold via an employee ownership trust . <p> A new Crown corporation to get homes built <p> Bill C-20 , the Build Canada Homes Act , turns the federal affordable housing agency launched last September into a Crown corporation . <p> The bill has passed third reading in the House of Commons and is expected to be up for consideration at committee and a final reading in the Senate . <p> This legislation gives Build Canada Homes the power to own , develop , transfer and finance property for development -- part of Liberals ' plan to scale up non-market housing in the country . <p> It also allows Build Canada Homes to take over property rights held by the Canada Land Company , another Crown corporation that stewards federal lands . <p> Three @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ MP Frank Caputo 's bill C-225 passed with widespread support and received royal assent earlier this month . <p> The law will amend the Criminal Code to allow the killer of an intimate partner to be charged with first-degree murder regardless of whether the act was premeditated . <p> The legislation is named Bailey 's Law after Bailey McCourt , a 32-year-old B.C. woman and mother of two who was killed last year . Her alleged killer was a former partner who was released on bail hours before the daylight attack at a Kelowna parking lot . <p> Ontario Conservative MP Adam Chambers ' bill C-230 also passed unanimously and is now before the Senate . <p> The bill would create a public registry of companies which receive tax writeoffs from the federal government worth more than $2 million . The original bill proposed a threshold of $1 million but it was amended at the committee stage . <p> Alberta Conservative MP Ziad Aboultaif also saw his bill C-234 pass . It would allow the Governor General to award a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Arab Heritage month <p> The House of Commons also passed two Senate bills . <p> Bill S-228 , which received royal assent earlier this week , criminalizes forced or coerced sterilization . The law says sterilization without legal consent constitutes aggravated assault , which carries a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison . <p> And S-227 passed Thursday as part of the motion to adjourn for the summer . The bill designates April as Arab Heritage Month across Canada . <p> " I wanted to thank all members of the House , " Liberal MP Ahmed Hussen said in the Commons while rising on a point of order . <p> " This is a really important bill for the community and for Canada and I really wanted to express my sincere gratitude to all colleagues . @@138281638 <p> Donald Trump has always borne the marks of the classic political " strongman . " An arrogant , vindictive egotist , who showers favours on his relatives and cronies while trying to squash anyone who dares to question him , he is a caricature of the type . <p> With his disastrous deal to end his disastrous war with Iran , Mr. Trump has shown he has another of the common characteristics of that unfortunate breed . He is a serial bungler . <p> Asked to weigh the respective advantages of democratic and authoritarian government , many people would say that the authoritarian kind is nastier , but more efficient . Yes , strongmen throw their rivals in jail , fill their pockets with stolen money and hold on to power long past their time -- but , darn it , they get things done . Did n't Mussolini make the trains run on time ? <p> The reality is quite different . Undemocratic regimes are , in most cases , horribly inefficient . Decades of Soviet rule in Russia and Eastern Europe left broken economies , crumbling roads @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduced Latin America 's richest nation to one of its poorest . <p> Worse , authoritarian rulers tend to make calamitous mistakes . Surrounded by yes-men , shielded from reality , fawned over by a complaisant media , certain of their infallibility , they stumble blindly into error . <p> Even as Hitler marshalled division upon division on Soviet borders , Stalin simply refused to believe he would break their non-aggression pact . The German attack was only turned back after millions of Russians lay dead . Japan 's ruling clique made war on the world 's richest and most dynamic nation when it attacked Pearl Harbor . The outcome was inevitable . <p> Mao inflicted a deadly famine on the struggling Chinese people when he launched the Great Leap Forward . Herding peasants into giant communes , he ordered them to bang pots and pans together to make grain-stealing sparrows drop from exhaustion . The most recent of many examples is that archetypal strong man , Vladimir Putin , the bare-chested horseman , who plunged Russia into a pointless war with Ukraine that has made his nation an international @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we still tend to think of strongmen as sharp , if brutal , operators . The main aims of this enormously costly and destructive war were to end Iran 's nuclear program ; make it stop supporting militant proxies in Lebanon , Gaza , Iraq and Yemen ; destroy its ballistic missile force and , ideally , end the Iranian regime altogether . At the peak of his belligerence , Mr. Trump demanded nothing less than its " UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER . ( Jacob King/PA Images via Getty Images ) <p> ( JTA ) -- TEL AVIV -- More than five decades after Israel 's only World Cup appearance , the Israel Football Association says it has no intention of trying to leave Europe for the Asian regional qualifying system that once took the country to the tournament , before Arab-led boycotts helped force it out . <p> The launch this month of the tournament hosted by the United States , Mexico and Canada has renewed attention to Israel 's absence from the World Cup . Despite a thriving local soccer scene and success in competition abroad , the only time the country appeared in the tournament was in Mexico in 1970 . <p> That 's because Israel seeks to qualify through the Union @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that even a solid campaign can become a long shot for the World Cup . Even titans like four-time World Cup winner Italy failed to qualify this year . <p> Israel is the only non-European country trying to reach the tournament through UEFA , while most of its neighbours seek places through the Asian Football Confederation . Israel was ousted from the Asian soccer body in 1974 . It bounced around the qualifying zones for a few years -- it played in the Oceania qualifiers ahead of the 1986 and 1990 World Cups -- before settling in the European grouping in 1991 . <p> Shlomi Barzel , head of communications for the Israel Football Association , said a return to Asia is not on the table , both because Israel does not want to leave European soccer , where it has built a standing , and because he does not believe the Asian confederation would accept it back . <p> The only upside to such a move , he joked , would be if Israel 's opponents boycotted matches against it : " Israel would automatically qualify . " <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the 1970 World Cup . North Korea was ejected from the Asian qualifying tournament after refusing to play in Israel . As a result , Israel advanced to the final round after winning only two games against New Zealand . In the finals , Israel faced an Australian team already exhausted after fending off South Korea , Japan and Rhodesia ( itself in the Asian tournament after being banned in Africa over its white governing regime ) . <p> In the tournament in Mexico , Israel 's all-amateur team defied expectations , losing 0-2 to Uruguay but notching draws against Sweden and Italy before being eliminated . <p> Four years later , Israel was effectively ejected from the Asian Football Confederation following a resolution introduced by Kuwait that passed 17 to 13 , with six abstentions . The vote came a day before a high-profile Israel-Iran game in Tehran that Iran won 1-0 on an Israeli own goal . <p> Today , Barzel rejects the premise that rejoining the AFC would guarantee Israel a place in the World Cup going forward . <p> " It would be a little @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he said , adding that he was not sure Israel would beat teams such as Jordan or Qatar . <p> Barzel also cited Israel 's place inside UEFA 's institutions as a benefit for sticking with the current arrangement . Current IFA chairman Moshe " Shino " Zuaretz was elected to UEFA 's Executive Committee in April 2025 , despite the war in Gaza and growing calls to sanction Israeli soccer , while former IFA chairman Avi Luzon previously served in a senior role on the same body . <p> Institutional backing has extended beyond Europe , Barzel said , pointing to the 2022 World Cup in Qatar , where Israeli fans were allowed to attend despite the absence of diplomatic ties . He also cited the global soccer body FIFA 's decision to move the 2023 under-20s World Cup from Indonesia to Argentina after Indonesia objected to hosting Israel 's team . Israel went on to finish third . <p> Still , Israel 's formal place in international soccer has done little to shield its teams and supporters from hostility . That looks like investing in education , housing , climate resilient infrastructure and healthcare , instead of a cruel and abusive detention system . ( Supplied photo ) <p> In the hours before Shabbat last month , 300 Jews from across British Columbia converged on the mountain town of Whistler for Jewish Federation 's 2026 Community Engagement Summit . There were families , couples , seniors and volunteers from dozens of regional B.C. communities . It looked like any other gathering for a family-friendly Shabbat and weekend conference . But for some of the 50 children racing together across the grass , this was entirely new : It was the first time in their lives that they had been surrounded by a group of Jewish peers . <p> The scene captured the real story behind the Jewish Federation of Greater Vancouver 's expansion this week into the Jewish Federation of British Columbia ( JFBC ) . While the change broadens the organization 's mandate , leaders say the larger transformation is about helping @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ needed to thrive . <p> In the process , JFBC is making history : This is the first time a Jewish Federation in a major Canadian population centre has widened its focus from its city home base to the entire province . The recent summit was an example of what happens when small Jewish communities gain access to resources , expertise and connections that previously existed only in larger urban centres . <p> " These can become self-sufficient , vibrant Jewish communities , " said Ezra Shanken , CEO of JFBC . <p> A new map of Jewish life <p> For generations , organized Jewish life in Western Canada revolved around a handful of major cities . That geography is changing . <p> The 2021 Canadian census showed that the Jewish population of B.C. , around 44,000 , is steadily moving away from Vancouver and the rest of the Lower Mainland , and toward areas including Vancouver Island and B.C. 's interior . Growth throughout B.C. is outpacing the national average several times over : Canada 's Jewish population grew by about 5 per cent and Vancouver 's by 14 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Vancouver jumped by 60 per cent . B.C. 's capital city of Victoria is currently seeing the fastest Jewish population growth in the country . <p> Like other Canadians , Jewish families are increasingly moving outward in search of a lower cost of living , recreation opportunities and the flexibility offered by remote work , settling in places like Vancouver Island , the Okanagan , and the Sea-to-Sky corridor . Many are seeking a different lifestyle , but unlike previous generations , they want to remain connected to organized Jewish life <p> " We 're still seeing people wanting to be more and more connected , wanting to belong , " said JFBC chief planning officer Mijal Ben-Dori . <p> From isolation to community <p> The Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7 , 2023 and the war in Gaza , along with the rise of antisemitism in Canada have intensified that drive for connection . Across North America , many Jews have sought stronger ties to community , identity and security . " <p> " Though Yellowknife falls outside the jurisdiction of any Federation , JFBC stepped in to support the fledgling community . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an outsized impact . " These can become self-sufficient , vibrant Jewish communities . " <p> The Connector model <p> The strategy behind the new JFBC is rooted in the idea that healthy communities are built through relationships , rather than through infrastructure . The main pillar of this strategy is a growing network of Community Connectors . <p> The program began several years ago @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ regions throughout the province . These part-time connectors identify unaffiliated Jews , introduce newcomers to existing networks , support local volunteers , help communities access Federation resources and connect isolated regions to the broader Jewish world . <p> The model emerged after years of major Jewish organizations relying on a " hub-and-spoke " model , sending staff from large cities into smaller communities on a temporary basis . While those efforts had some value , it was difficult to develop lasting local leadership or to best meet the needs of individual communities . <p> Instead of importing solutions , connectors work within communities to help residents create their own . <p> " Sending people from Vancouver can only go so far , " Ben-Dori said . " We need to have people ( already ) in these communities to grow the community . " <p> The results have been striking . The network has already supported more than 200 events this year alone -- more than double that of 2025 -- and more than 8,000 participants in total . The broadcast was temporarily shutdown due to public safety concerns . <p> Updated 5 hrs ago <h> Drone wars : Toronto police have one eye on the skies , as the FIFA World Cup plays out on the ground <p> Toronto police continue to remind people that unauthorized drones are not allowed in the restricted airspaces around stadiums , team sites , FIFA Fan Festival and other secured areas . <p> Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press Toronto Star <p> Attempts by fans and tourists to capture sweeping images of the excitement at World Cup venues across North America may be innocent , but security agencies are treating it as an issue of national security . <p> To date , Toronto police have intercepted 17 unauthorized drones over restricted airspace around Toronto Stadium and the nearby fan zone , doling out fines and charging two people with reckless operation , including one tourist from Turkey . U.S. law enforcement agencies say they 've seized dozens of drones around the stadiums of the 11 U.S. host cities . <p> Drone use is governed by Canadian aviation regulations set forth by Transport Canada . Violating those regulations , which establish when and where drones can be flown and by whom , can carry fines that range from $1,000 to $5,000 . According to the transportation agency , the restricted airspace over the Toronto venues at Exhibition Place has a radius of about 2.4 km ( 1.3 nautical miles ) . <p> " Unauthorized drones are not permitted in restricted airspace around Toronto Stadium , FIFA Fan Festival , team sites and other secured areas , " said Toronto police in an emailed statement . This includes airspace over practice pitches at Centennial Park in Etobicoke . <p> There 's been a huge shift in accessibility and regulations in the past 20 years , said Pedram Nowroozi , the CEO of InfinitDrones , a company based in Woodbridge that manufactures drone detection equipment . <p> " There were no laws , there were no regulations , " he said . " But now that they 're becoming so much more affordable , the government 's taking the time to make sure everyone 's doing it safely . " <p> While Toronto police would not divulge details on how they 're intercepting drones due to security issues , the Star spoke with experts about how drone detection technology works and the difficulty of patrolling the vast exclusion area around Toronto 's World Cup matches . <h> How are drones being intercepted ? <p> Nowroozi said he works with 80 per cent of Canadian emergency response organizations such as OPP , RCMP and local police agencies across the province , including in Toronto . <p> Detection technology " sniffs " out the radio frequency transmitted by a drone which can determine three basic things : where the drone is in the sky , the point from which the drone took off ( known as the " home point " ) and where the remote controller is . <p> Once the remote has been located , individuals are located and asked to fly the drone down . <p> This requires co-operation on behalf of the manufacturer , which shares this radio signal for emergency response scenarios to prevent " rogue drones . " <p> Mitigation systems , which can either take over a drone or push it back to its home point , can only be sold to the RCMP . <h> Hobby drones and black ops <p> While regular consumer drones are easy to detect and intercept , some drones are off the grid , said Alex Ferworn , a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies computational public safety . <p> " There are hand-held devices that police have that enable them to determine what type of drone is actually being flown , as long as it 's made by a manufacturer that has registered that drone , " said Ferworn . " The problem comes when you 're in the hobbyist world . " <p> Hobbyists who make their own drones , he said , may not be operating on standard frequencies , making mitigation difficult . <p> Alex Ferworn in 2012 testing out a drone , hovering overhead . <p> Supplied Toronto Star <p> " ( Police ) might be able to detect it because they know that radio traffic is happening , but they ca n't do anything about actually stopping it , " said Ferworn , explaining that attempts to " jam " the signal could disrupt all signals on the frequency -- of which there are likely many in a big city like Toronto . <p> The professor said another potential problem are drones with predetermined flight paths -- with no remote controller , there is no radio frequency being transmitted . <p> " This is the dark drone , sometimes called the black ops drone , " he said . " They simply fly and they do n't return to sender . " <p> In special circumstances , he said , mitigation might involve deploying a net to capture a drone , which disables its rotors to bring it down . <h> What we know about drones near the FIFA Fan Festival <p> Police have yet to confirm how far into the no-drone zone unmanned aircraft have flown since the start of the World Cup , but they have disclosed the approximate locations of the operators violating restricted air space over the FIFA events . <p> While officials said the operators have mostly been excited fans , they are n't concerned with their intent , however innocent it may be . <p> " Drones can create significant safety and security risks in the context of a major international event , " Toronto police wrote in an email to the Star . " They can disrupt operations , impact public safety and interfere with aviation and emergency response activities . " <p> Police said that all drones that were intercepted were returned to their owners , noting that seizure of the equipment would only occur in the case of a serious enforcement action , such as a criminal investigation . <p> " The easiest way to avoid enforcement action is simple , " they wrote , " know the rules and follow them . " <p> A reminder for fans with gadgets ! Drones are not permitted above or around Centennial Park -- no exceptions .
